DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Food Waste Collection

The pilot design is sound, and most of the arithmetic checks out. However, three of the study's central claims don't survive a check against its own figures:
- The pilot does **not** show similar participation in houses and flats.
- The district projection uses a participation rate the pilot never produced.
- Brookfield can only take about **half** the projected tonnage.

Once these are corrected, the £490,000 net cost rises, and the claim that the service is "fully covered" by the £520,000 allocation no longer holds.

## Major issues

### 1. Participation in flats is a third of the rate in houses

Table 1 shows:

| Housing type | Participation |
|---|---|
| Houses | **66%** |
| Flats | **21%** |

That is not "broadly similar." Flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses. The table is internally consistent (2,112/3,200, 168/800 and 2,280/4,000 are all correct), so the text conclusion is what's wrong.

This matters for the recommendation. About 20% of the district's households are flats, and the pilot is clear evidence that a uniform service underperforms there. Most councils need a different approach for flats, such as communal bins, bin-store placement, and targeted engagement. The study should recommend that, not rule it out.

### 2. The projection uses 64% participation, but the pilot found 57%

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate," but no 64% appears anywhere in the pilot data:
- The pilot's overall rate was **57%**.
- The pilot's housing mix (20% flats) matches the district's, so 57% can be applied directly.

| | Tonnes a year |
|---|---|
| As written (64%, 1.9 kg) | **3,290** |
| Pilot rates by housing type (houses 66% × 1.9 kg; flats 21% × 1.4 kg) | **about 2,870** |

The projection is overstated by about 13%, and so is the disposal saving: about £212,000 a year on the corrected tonnage, not £243,000.

### 3. Brookfield can only take 1,800 tonnes

Section 4 confirms Brookfield's contracted capacity is **1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected projection of about 2,870 tonnes leaves roughly **1,000 tonnes a year with no costed destination**.

- The study prices the whole tonnage at Brookfield's £38 gate fee.
- The surplus would have to go to the plant **46 miles away**, at an unstated gate fee plus significant extra haulage: extra vehicle time, fuel, and possibly a transfer station.
- Leaving it in the residual bin isn't a compliant option, since the point of the service is separate collection and treatment.
- "Treatment is local" is therefore true for only about 60% of the tonnage.

### 4. The service is not shown to be fully funded

At Brookfield's terms, the saving on the 1,800 tonnes it can take is 1,800 × £74 = **£133,200**. The remaining tonnage has an unknown net cost.

| | Annual |
|---|---|
| Total cost (Table 2) | £733,400 |
| Saving on 1,800 t at Brookfield | −£133,200 |
| **Net cost before the surplus tonnage** | **£600,200** |

Whether the remaining ~1,000 tonnes produce any further saving depends on the second plant's gate fee and haulage cost, which haven't been quantified. On these figures, the net cost is likely to exceed the **£520,000** provisional allocation.

Even on the study's own numbers, the margin was only £30,000, or 6%. And the allocation is described as "provisional," which the Government has merely "indicated." "Fully funded" overstates the certainty in both respects.

### 5. The cost lines aren't complete

The totals add up correctly:
- Vehicles: 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 years ≈ £141,400
- Crews: 12 × £34,000 = £408,000
- Total: £733,400, and £733,400 − £243,000 ≈ £490,000

But several items are missing:
- **Capital outlay.** Buying six vehicles needs about **£990,000 up front** in 2026/27. Annual depreciation doesn't reflect that, and there's no financing cost. The study doesn't say how the upfront purchase will be funded.
- **Haulage** to the second plant (see point 3).
- **Crew cover** for leave and sickness, supervision, and agency staff. Twelve operatives for six vehicles assumes no absence.
- **One-off launch costs:** caddy delivery logistics, the dedicated phone line, and recruitment.
- **Ongoing liners** beyond the initial three-month supply. These may be included in the £88,000, but that should be stated.

## Smaller issues

- **Satisfaction figure.** The 81% is from "surveyed pilot households." If the survey mostly reached participants, it says little about the 43% who didn't take part, which is where the improvement potential lies.
- **Pilot timing.**
  - Participation often falls once a scheme's novelty wears off, and six months may not capture that.
  - Food waste volumes also vary seasonally.
  - A note on the week-by-week trend within the pilot would help.
- **Average yield.** The "All" figure of 1.9 kg is really 1.86 kg when weighted. That rounds correctly, but the per-housing-type figures should be used in the projection, as above.
- **Brookfield contract.** The study refers to a confirmed capacity offer but not to a contract or procurement route. That needs to be in place before April 2027.
- **After 2029.** Brookfield's expansion may resolve the capacity issue then, but the study needs a costed plan for 2027–2029.
- **Timetable.** This is the strongest section. December ordering for March delivery is tight but workable, provided Cabinet approval comes in time.

## What holds up

- The pilot design: 4,000 households across mixed wards, measured weekly by housing type.
- The internal consistency of Table 1 and the cost arithmetic in Table 2.
- The gate fee comparison, which gives a genuine £74/tonne saving for tonnage that Brookfield can take.
- Low contamination (under 2%) and falling missed-collection reports, which are good operational signals.

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct section 2's text: participation differed sharply by housing type. Add a flats-specific approach to the roll-out.
2. Recalculate tonnage using the pilot's actual rates (about 2,870 t), split by housing type.
3. Cost the ~1,000 tonnes above Brookfield's capacity, including haulage to the 46-mile plant, and show the 2027–2029 position separately from later years.
4. Add the upfront capital requirement and its funding source, crew cover, and one-off launch costs.
5. Restate the funding position as a range against the provisional allocation, with the size of any gap the Council may need to cover.

The roll-out is a legal requirement, so the question for Cabinet is less whether to go ahead than on what terms. As written, though, the study shouldn't tell members the service is evidenced as uniform across housing types or fully funded. On the corrected figures, it's likely to need Council funding on top of the allocation, at least until 2029.
